R6-S19.title: Effects of Short- and Long-Term Detraining on Maximal Oxygen Uptake in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
R6-S19.authors: Zheng J, Pan T, Jiang Y, Shen Y
R6-S19.population_design_dose: 21 studies of trained individuals after training cessation.
R6-S19.findings: VO2max decreased after short-term (ES -0.62) and more after long-term cessation (ES -1.42).
limitations: VO2max only; heterogeneous definitions of short/long; athletes.
counterevidence: No difference between 30-90 and >90 days in subgroup analysis.

R6-S21.title: Individualized Endurance Training Based on Recovery and Training Status in Recreational Runners
R6-S21.authors: Nuuttila OP, Nummela A, Korhonen E, Hakkinen K, Kyrolainen H
R6-S21.population_design_dose: 30 recreational runners, matched-pair randomized, 15 wk; predefined program (2 progressive weeks with +10% volume then a -25% recovery week) versus load adjusted twice weekly from HRV, perceived recovery and HR-speed index.
R6-S21.findings: Both groups improved; individualized group improved 10-km time more (-6.2% versus -2.9%) with fewer low responders; HIT block used 6x3 min at maximal sustainable effort.
limitations: Small sample; HRV-dependent monitoring; negligible strength training.

R6-S02.title: How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study
R6-S02.authors: Schuster Brandt Frandsen J, Hulme A, Parner ET, Moller M, Lindman I, Abrahamson J, et al., Nielsen RO
R6-S02.population_design_dose: 5205 adult runners (mean 45.8 y, 22% female), Garmin GPS data, 588,071 sessions, 18-month follow-up; exposure = single-session distance relative to the longest run in the previous 30 days.
R6-S02.findings: Single-session spikes >10-30%, >30-100% and >100% above the 30-day longest run were associated with higher overuse-injury rates (HRR 1.64, 1.52, 2.28); week-to-week ratio showed no association and ACWR an inverse one.
R6-S02.locator: Abstract; Methods (exposure definition); Results Table 1; Discussion, Limitations.
limitations: Observational; authors state a preventive 10% rule needs randomized evidence.
Distance, not duration; self-reported injury; binned, non-monotonic hazard ratios.
counterevidence: Weekly progression metrics were not associated with injury in the same cohort.
